title: SMPP request/response tracking
description:
Wanted to do this more than 15+ years ago... now features in wmem have made it easier :smile: 
Tested with pcaps containing:
- Normal bidirectional SMPP traffic
- Reused sequence numbers
- Mismatched request
- Mismatched response

Plan to add SRT in another pull request.

This "leaks" too much memory.  You're creating file scoped keys every time a packet is dissected, but they only need to persist on the first pass, i.e. !PINFO_FD_VISITED(pinfo).  You should find a better way to create a "temporary" key for lookup in the table.

In general, I had thought the same about the keys - in theory, they should be needed only during processing of the current frame. So, I had tried with scope pinfo->pool scope instead, but for reasons beyond my understanding, it doesn't work.

The key is also needed for the lookup after the first pass... for displaying the conversation details.

I saw wmem_file_scope being used for the same purpose in other dissectors for the same/similar purpose (e.g. packet-mgcp.c: new_mgcp_call_key, packet-gsm_sms.c: p_frag_params_key), and hence left it as-is. 

I will try again once to see if I can make it work without allocating in file scope.
The key needs to be file-scoped when adding to the multimap (the key value there is saved and not copied), but all other places it should be pinfo->pool scoped.
Thanks for the explanation, Michael! Addressed in updated (squashed) commit.
Should also squash your commits into a single one for final submission.

This does not initialize `smpp_txn->res_frame`, but you may end up testing against its value in line 2677 and 2686. It is probably safest to use `wmem_new0`, or you could explicitly initialize it to 0.

See issue #20891

Forgive my ignorance, but seeing as this one MR is already merged, do I have to open a new one or can I still update this one.

I specifically tested the cases where the capture had only a request or a response and it didn't cause a problem - I must be missing something...

You have to open a new one.

So in practice in most cases the memory will happen to be initialized to zero there so it will work in testing. It's just a violation of the C standard so there's no guarantee that it's zero.
